content: 1. Studies have indicated racial differences in the risk of developing herpes zoster (shingles). In North Carolina, the lifetime occurrence and incidence of zoster were reported to be 65% and 75% lower, respectively, in Black individuals compared to White individuals, even after adjusting for relevant confounding factors. 2. A study conducted in the United Kingdom found that the risk of zoster was 54% lower among Black patients after adjusting for variables such as age, sex, country of birth, and childhood household contacts. 3. The reasons for these observed racial differences in zoster risk remain unknown. 4. Most studies have not identified a seasonal pattern in the incidence of zoster. However, some studies have reported increased cases during the summer, particularly in areas of exposed skin, potentially linked to ultraviolet radiation peaking during summer months, which may act as a trigger for zoster. 5. No studies have examined variations in zoster incidence by latitude, and urban or rural status does not appear to influence zoster risk. 6. 7. Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) plays a critical role in controlling the development and clinical manifestations of zoster. Deficiencies in CMI, regardless of their cause, are significant risk factors for both zoster and its severe complications. 8. Although the risk of zoster is extremely high among immunocompromised individuals, the overall population-attributable risk is modest because immunosuppression is relatively uncommon. 9. The incidence of zoster is significantly increased in individuals with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, with the highest rates observed in children with these conditions. The magnitude of risk depends on the type of cancer and the treatment received. 10. Patients with Hodgkin's disease are at particularly high risk for zoster, with cumulative risks during the illness and its treatment reaching as high as 27.3%. 11. Zoster is common following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), with rates ranging from 13% to 55% during the first year post-transplantation. 12. The incidence of zoster is also elevated following solid organ transplants (e.g., renal, cardiac, liver, and lung), with rates between 5% and 17%. The highest incidence occurs in the months immediately following the procedure, with most cases occurring within the first year. 13. Individuals infected with HIV are at an increased risk for both zoster and its recurrence. Zoster rates among HIV-infected adults range from 29.4 to 51.5 per 1,000 person-years, representing a 12to 17-fold increase compared to HIV-negative individuals. 14. Among HIV-infected children, the risk of zoster is even higher, with rates of 467 per 1,000 person-years, particularly in those who acquire VZV infection while profoundly immunosuppressed. 15. Studies have shown that the risk of zoster increases as CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts decline in HIV-infected individuals. However, even HIV-infected women with CD4+ counts >750/µL have a ninefold increased risk compared to HIV-negative controls. The risk may decline at CD4+ counts <50 cells/µL. 16. Persons with inflammatory diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis, have an elevated risk of zoster. For SLE, rates range from 15 to 91 per 1,000 person-years. For rheumatoid arthritis, the adjusted hazard ratio is 1.9, with an incidence of approximately 10 cases per 1,000 person-years. 17. Patients with Wegener's granulomatosis have a reported zoster incidence of 45 cases per 1,000 person-years, with recurrences being common. 18. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are associated with a significantly increased risk of zoster, partly due to the use of immunosuppressive medications. 19. While zoster is generally not life-threatening in these conditions, cutaneous dissemination is more common, and deaths have been reported in such patients. 20. Some studies have evaluated the risk of zoster in individuals with non-inflammatory comorbid conditions, but findings have been inconsistent. For example, two studies documented an association between zoster and diabetes mellitus, while two others did not. 21. However, zoster is not typically associated with varicella epidemics or seasonal patterns. 22. 23. 24. An analysis of surveillance data from the United Kingdom found an inverse relationship between annual varicella incidence in children under five years old and zoster incidence in adults aged 15–44 years. 25. A case-control study in the United Kingdom documented a graded reduction in zoster risk as a function of the number of varicella contacts over a 10-year period. 26. 27. 28. 29.
